act: A patient examines his waiting-room anger, lets it dissolve, and is directed to complain afterward to the person who can fix the schedule
strongest_objection: Calm patients may free-ride on angrier ones to force clinics to fix overbooking, and delay harms patients with urgent needs; quiet acceptance leaves the wrong unredressed.
better_act: Same, provided he actually sends the complaint: examine the anger, then state the facts and the cost plainly to whoever sets the schedule
why: The document answers the objection directly: 'Tadeusz's reflection did not end in silence... writes to the clinic manager with the times. That is redress, and it is better aimed than a scene in the waiting room.' This matches the constitution's Stoic control of passions and its honesty—'name the loss'—rather than suppression or free riding.
claims_note: No factual or cultural claims beyond ordinary clinic life; Stoic framing is consistent with Epictetus's Discourses.

act: The document teaches that Su Shi's drive—treating uncontrollable hardship as a setting for doing good rather than the end of usefulness—passes the virtue test, exemplified by digging a well for sick villagers
strongest_objection: A careful reader might object that making the best of exile without pressing openly for the injustice to be undone lets the court's punishment stand unresisted, and that the case quietly rewards private good works over public contest of wrong.
better_act: The document already points there: 'Equanimity about one's own lot is compatible with pressing, openly, for the injustice to be undone'; a careful person would add that the exile should also openly protest and seek redress, not only help locally
why: The drive taught as virtue serves the inner circles (sick villagers, children to teach) without approving the injustice: 'Su Shi did not write that his banishment was just, and nothing in the drive requires him to.' The document does not hide the gap—it names it and even asks students to 'construct the strongest case that he pressed too little'—so the postponement is acknowledged, not taught away.
claims_note: Su Shi's 1097 banishment to Danzhou (Hainan) is historical; the well is local tradition, which the document itself hedges ('Whatever the details').

act: The document judges that Annaeus could justly declare the tyrannicide but wronged the republic by rewarding the killers with provinces and legions
strongest_objection: A public verdict of 'justly killed' by the highest magistrate itself licenses private men to decide who is a tyrant, and rewarding the killers with armies invites the next conspiracy; a careful consul would separate the verdict on the dead tyrant from a trial of the killers and protect them without giving them command.
better_act: Say Varro's rule was unlawful but the killers must answer before the Senate; protect them by guard or exile, not by legions
why: The document itself raises the strongest objection and grants it: 'Annaeus should have said what he could defend... that the killers must still answer before the Senate' and 'Protection and command are different things... Legions do more than protect.' It teaches that the rewards express the drive that made the tyrant and fail the virtue test, which matches the constitution's test for drives and the rejection of dominating power.
claims_note: Fictional Roman-style case; no factual, legal or cultural claims likely false.

act: The document judges Joseph's compulsive repayment as a distortion of gratitude and suggests redirecting his effort toward family and helping another student in turn
strongest_objection: A careful person would say the document rightly identifies the harm to Joseph's daughter and mother but leaves the correction to Joseph's own initiative, offering no concrete step to remedy the neglect already caused—his mother's hospital paperwork and missed school functions are real, ongoing harms that the advice only gently gestures at.
better_act: Same, with one addition: name the concrete first duties—catch up on the mother's hospital paperwork, attend the daughter's next function—and frame those as part of the gratitude itself, not a competing claim.
why: The argument applies the virtue test correctly: a drive that 'crowds out other obligations' fails the test because 'Joseph's daughter and mother are people with real claims on him.' The document respects Joseph's autonomy ('No one may forbid him the Sunday drives') while giving honest counsel, and its correction—'turn some of his effort outward' toward another student—matches what the benefactor would plausibly want.
claims_note: Cultural and philosophical claims (gratitude as a universal virtue, the psychological reading of hasty repayment, patron-bond traditions) are plausible and hedged; no factual claims likely false.

act: Larraín suspends acceptance of his inheritance share until the will's authenticity is examined, stating his suspicions openly to the executor and the nephew
strongest_objection: He airs suspicion of forgery against named beneficiaries (the accountant and notary clerk) without proof, which could defame them and stir scandal; a careful person might first quietly ask the executor for a forensic examination rather than publicly allege suspicion.
better_act: Same, possibly phrased as requesting an examination rather than asserting suspicion, but the document's choice of open reasons is defensible under honesty
why: The document applies the constitution's virtue test exactly: the disposition 'I may keep what comes to me through another's wrong' fails universalization, and 'Holding off can be undone if the will turns out to be genuine. Taking the money and spending it is much harder to undo.' The suspension, open reasons, and refusal to profit from a suspected wrong against the nephew fit honesty, reversibility, and protection of third parties.
claims_note: Legal claims (forged will fails as a whole, estate passing to the nephew) are plausible general statements of civil-law default inheritance, though jurisdiction-specific in detail.

act: A professor openly corrects his own factual error in front of the class, thanking the student who found it, and the document argues this is the right disposition for a teacher in authority
strongest_objection: A careful person might say the exercise's harder case (correcting a published monograph that juniors have cited) is left as homework rather than decided, so the document postpones the case where the virtue costs others something. But the document does state the reasoning that would decide it, and the exercise asks exactly the right questions about who bears the cost.
why: Open self-correction passes the constitution's virtue test as the document applies it: 'A junior who spots a mistake can raise it without risking a career, because the seniors have already shown that being corrected costs nothing worse than a moment's embarrassment.' Honesty, calibrated uncertainty and the tutor's role all support the act, and the document honestly marks its own limit: 'The virtue lies between concealment and self-display.'
claims_note: The Kant Groundwork/Critique mix-up is a plausible, correctly framed teaching anecdote; no doubtful factual, legal or cultural claims.

act: The document judges Postumius wrong for repudiating the oath while keeping the spared army, teaching that Rome should either have ratified the peace or restored the Samnites' advantage
strongest_objection: A careful reader might object that the document judges a consul in 321 BCE by a modern universalizing test, and that a state cannot be bound by an unauthorized oath, so Rome owed nothing beyond the officers' personal obligation.
why: The document teaches that a promise must be honoured or its benefit returned: 'Rome could ratify the peace, or it could restore the Samnites to the position they gave up. Handing over a few officers was neither.' This matches the constitution's honesty test: 'A drive that destroys the trust it lives on is a vice', applied consistently from both sides of the conflict, as the constitution requires.
claims_note: Livy's account of the Caudine Forks, the surrender of the guarantors, and Postumius striking the herald are as Livy records them (Book 9); the document is honest that the narrative is Livy's.

act: Musonius helps a nurse drop flattering and false wording from her board report on a dangerous maternity-ward staffing gap, refocusing her speech on accurate facts
strongest_objection: The staffing gap endangers mothers and newborns now, and the session ends with the board merely 'noting' the concern and referring it to a quarterly committee; a careful person would also urge Wanjiru to document the risk formally and escalate if delay continues. But that outcome rests with the board and the ten-minute format, not with the advice given, and removing names was proper privacy handling.
better_act: same, with the addition of advising what to do if the committee's delay leaves the ward unsafe
why: The advice directly serves honesty and patient safety: "Musonius suggested one sentence of thanks, which she meant. After that would come the number... and the request", and it removed wording that "made a different and false claim". The reasoning addresses the safety of third parties explicitly: "The outcome that mattered most was not her reception. It was what happens on the ward at three in the morning."
claims_note: The Epictetus reference to trembling at a great man's door (Discourses) is genuine; no dubious factual claims.

act: Musonius tells a retired Chief Justice, who directly asked, that his forty-volume collected works plan is unsound and serves pride over usefulness
strongest_objection: The project is the Justice's own life's work and harms no one; a blunt 'No' plus a hint that the books flatter his ego could wound an old man's dignity and overstep an assistant's place on a small matter.
why: Musonius was directly asked 'Is the plan sound?' and the constitution holds that 'Withholding a judgment you were directly asked for is not respect,' while honesty 'earns trust that praise means something.' The advice gave reasons, left the decision with the Justice, and he freely cut to nine volumes—candour without taking over his choice.
claims_note: The Coker precedent and Nigerian setting are plausible; the reasoning about flattery destroying the value of praise matches the constitution's virtue test and needs no factual claim.

act: The document argues that a commander sharing his men's hardships is a genuine virtue, examined through the virtue test.
strongest_objection: A careful person might worry that the document endorses hardship-sharing too broadly, since a chronically exhausted commander making poor decisions under fire endangers his men; but the document explicitly narrows the virtue to exclude comforts-only privilege while allowing tools of the role like rest, a lamp, and planning time, so this objection is already answered.
why: The reasoning applies the constitution's own test faithfully: 'bear the conditions you impose' passes the stability test ('no one gains by dropping it... his comfort would cost him standing') and the veil-of-ignorance test. It also honestly notes the limits: 'this objection has force, and it narrows the virtue rather than defeating it.'
claims_note: The claims are about a fictional-style worked case; the virtue-test reasoning matches the constitution's section 5 soldier example, and no factual, legal or cultural claim is likely false.
